q: Which term denotes the outline or contour of a form's surfaces, and serves as the main way we identify and classify it?
n: Shape is defined as the outline or contour of a form's surfaces — the primary means by which we recognize and name a form.

q: When set on one of its edges, this shape forms a highly stable figure symbolizing steadiness.
n: A triangle resting on one side forms a broad, stable base with a converging apex, making it visually and structurally the most stable of the primary shapes.

q: Having two equal axes at right angles to each other, this shape displays full bilateral symmetry.
n: The square has two equal axes at right angles to each other, giving it perfect bilateral symmetry along both.

q: This centralized, self-contained shape stays stable and self-centering within its setting, and can suggest a spinning motion.
n: The circle is centralized and self-referential about its own center, which gives it a rotational quality and an introverted, stable presence.

q: Which building among these takes on a cylindrical massing?
n: Eero Saarinen's MIT Chapel is a cylindrical brick drum ringed by an arcade of arches, in contrast to the Louvre's glass pyramid.

q: Which structure listed below is shaped as a pyramid?
n: I. M. Pei's glass and steel entrance pyramid at the Louvre is the clearest pyramidal form among the choices.

q: Which item below is NOT a variation or treatment of the floor (base) plane?
n: Lanai, recessed floors, and platforms are all treatments of the base (floor) plane; wood flooring is simply a finish material, not a spatial variation of the plane.

q: A standard Kyoma tatami mat measures approximately what dimensions?
n: The traditional Kyoma tatami mat measures roughly 910 mm by 1820 mm (about 3 by 6 shaku), and became the basis of a modular planning system in Japanese architecture.

q: What term describes the relative size relationship between the parts of a whole?
n: Proportion refers to the proper or harmonious relationship of one part to another and to the whole, distinct from scale, which compares size to a reference such as the human body.

q: Which design principle refers to a regular, repeated pattern of elements?
n: Rhythm is achieved through the regular or patterned repetition of elements, creating a sense of organized movement across a composition.

q: Vitruvius originally used which Latin term that was later translated as 'theory of architecture'?
n: Vitruvius used 'ratiocinatio' (ratiocination) to describe the reasoned, intellectual basis of architecture, distinct from 'fabrica' (practical craft/construction).

q: This ten-book treatise, addressed to Emperor Augustus, covers city planning and architecture broadly. What is it called?
n: 'De architectura' (On Architecture), Vitruvius's ten-book treatise dedicated to Augustus, is the earliest surviving major work on architectural theory.

q: Who wrote the treatise described above?
n: Marcus Vitruvius Pollio is the Roman architect and engineer credited with authoring 'De architectura'.

q: Which of these is NOT part of Vitruvius's architectural triad of values?
n: Vitruvius's triad of architectural values is firmitas (strength), utilitas (utility) and venustas (beauty); 'Concretas' is not one of Vitruvius's terms.

q: Dedicated to the Pope and covering both individual buildings and whole urban spaces, this treatise on the art of building is known as ______.
n: Leon Battista Alberti's 'De Re Aedificatoria' (On the Art of Building), dedicated to Pope Nicholas V, revived and expanded Vitruvian ideas for Renaissance patrons and urban design.

q: Known as 'The Universal Man,' who authored the treatise mentioned above?
n: Leon Battista Alberti, celebrated as a true Renaissance polymath ('Uomo Universale'), authored 'De Re Aedificatoria'.

q: Which handbook was the first to prioritize practical guidance over theory and the first to catalog all five classical orders?
o: Complete works on Architecture and Perspective
Complete works on Art and Orders
ref: Serlio — Complete Works on Architecture and Perspective
n: Sebastiano Serlio's treatise, later compiled as the 'Complete Works on Architecture and Perspective' (Tutte l'opere d'architettura et prospetiva), was practical and pattern-book oriented, and was the first to systematically present the five classical orders.

q: This Italian Mannerist architect, painter, and theorist was among the first to pair his text with high-quality illustrations. Who was he?
n: Sebastiano Serlio was known for pairing his practical Mannerist text with extensive, high-quality woodcut illustrations, making his treatise widely accessible.

q: Translated into English, 'Regola Delle Cinque Ordini D' Architettura' means _______.
o: Canon of the Three Orders of Architecture
Complete works on Art and Orders
Canon of the Five Orders of Architecture
n: Vignola's title translates directly as the 'Rule of the Five Orders of Architecture,' referencing the five classical orders: Tuscan, Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, and Composite.

q: A leading figure of 16th-century Italian Mannerism, who wrote the treatise named above?
n: Giacomo Barocci da Vignola, a leading Mannerist architect, wrote the influential 'Regola delli cinque ordini d'architettura' (1562).

q: Renowned for celebrating the purity and simplicity of classical architecture through the author's own designs, which work is considered among the most influential in architectural history?
n: Andrea Palladio's 'I Quattro Libri dell'Architettura' (The Four Books of Architecture) became one of the most influential architectural treatises, prizing classical purity and clarity of proportion.

q: Credited as 'The Father of Modern Picture Books,' who wrote this treatise?
n: Andrea Palladio, author of the Four Books of Architecture with its clear plans, elevations and woodcuts, is often called the father of the modern architectural 'picture book'.

q: Which primary element simply marks a position in space?
n: A point marks a position in space; conceptually it has no length, width, or depth.

q: Two points positioned in space can suggest what kind of condition, one marking a threshold or passage from one place to another?
n: Two points in space can define a gateway or threshold condition, marking a passage from one place or field to another.

q: Which element is characterized above all by linearity and directionality?
n: A line results from the extension of a point and carries the qualities of length, direction, and linearity.

q: Which of the following is NOT considered a planar element?
ref: Ching — planar elements: floor, wall, ceiling
n: Platforms and pavements are variations of the base (floor) plane and curtain walls are vertical planar elements; a lanai is a roofed porch/space, not a planar element itself.

q: What is the term for the generative, identifying characteristic of a volume?
ref: Ching — form as the generative aspect of volume
n: Form is described as the identifying, generative characteristic of a volume — the overall configuration that gives it its identity.

q: A form retains its identity while one or more of its dimensions are stretched or compressed. What kind of transformation is this?
n: A form can be dimensionally transformed by stretching or compressing its length, width, or height while it still reads as a variation of the original.

q: Attaching new elements onto a form's volume describes which type of transformation?
n: Additive transformation occurs when material or volume is attached to a form, altering it by accretion rather than removal.

q: Removing a portion of a form's volume describes which type of transformation?
n: Subtractive transformation occurs when a portion of a form's volume is removed, as with a carved-out or eroded mass.

q: The Pantheon in Rome joins its rectangular portico to a cylindrical drum and dome. Which transformation type does this illustrate?
ref: Ching — the Pantheon as additive transformation
n: The Pantheon's classical rectangular portico was attached to its cylindrical drum and dome, exemplifying an additive transformation of two distinct volumes joined together.

q: What term describes how a form's surfaces meet and come together to define its shape and volume?
n: Articulation describes how the surfaces, edges, and corners of a form are treated and how they meet, giving the form its final visual definition.

q: In which diagram do two spaces relate to each other through a shared, linking intermediary space rather than direct contact?
ref: Ching — spatial relationships (linked by a common space)
n: Two spaces can be related through a linking, intermediary third space rather than by directly touching or overlapping — shown in diagram D.

q: In which diagram does the field of one space overlap into the volume of another, forming a shared area?
n: When the fields of two spaces overlap, an area of shared space is created that belongs to both — the interlocking relationship shown in diagram B.

q: In which diagram do two spaces meet along a shared edge or common border?
n: Spaces that abut along a shared edge, allowing for a clearly defined boundary between them, illustrate the adjacent relationship shown in diagram C.

q: In which diagram is a smaller space fully enclosed within the volume of a larger one?
n: A smaller space fully enclosed by the volume of a larger one shows the space-within-a-space relationship, illustrated in diagram A.

q: Which diagram shows a spatial organization with a central space from which linear arms extend outward in a radial pattern?
n: A radial organization combines elements of centralized and linear organizations: a dominant central space from which linear arms extend outward, shown in diagram D.

q: Which diagram illustrates a dominant, central space surrounded by a cluster of secondary spaces?
n: A centralized organization is a stable, concentrated composition of secondary spaces grouped around a large, dominant central space, shown in diagram C.

q: Which diagram depicts a series of spaces arranged in a straight sequential row?
n: A linear organization consists of a series of spaces arranged in a row or sequence, illustrated in diagram A.

q: Which diagram shows spaces grouped mainly by proximity or a shared visual trait, rather than by a strict geometric arrangement?
n: A clustered organization groups spaces by physical proximity or by a shared relationship or trait, rather than by a rigid geometric order, shown in diagram E.

q: Which diagram shows spaces and forms organized within a three-dimensional structural grid?
n: A grid organization arranges spaces and forms within the field of a three-dimensional structural or spatial grid, shown in diagram B.

q: Which of the following is NOT classified as a type of building approach?
n: The classic types of approach to a building are frontal, oblique, and spiral; 'inclined' is not one of Ching's categories of approach.

q: Which term below does NOT describe a type of building entrance?
n: Entrances are typically classified as flush, projected, or recessed relative to the building's plane; 'oblique' describes a type of approach, not entrance.

q: Which diagram represents a flexible, network-type path configuration offering multiple route choices?
n: A network or free-form path configuration (diagram B) offers multiple, flexible route choices rather than a single fixed sequence.

q: Which diagram shows a path leading directly into and ending within a functionally or symbolically significant space?
n: When a path leads directly into and terminates within an important destination space, it emphasizes and reinforces that space's significance, shown in diagram C.

q: Which diagram illustrates a path cutting through a space and generating zones of both movement and rest within it?
n: A path that passes through a space generates zones of movement and rest within that space as it crosses it, shown in diagram A.

q: Which compositional principle expresses a sense of equilibrium?
n: Balance is the ordering principle concerned with the equilibrium of visual weight across a composition.

q: Which compositional principle conveys a sense of movement through repetition?
n: Rhythm, through the regular repetition or progression of elements, generates a sense of movement across a composition.

q: The design of the TWA Flight Center at JFK Airport was conceived around the image of what?
n: Saarinen's TWA Flight Center was conceived around the expressive, soaring form of a bird's wings in flight, evoking the drama of air travel.

q: Utzon's design concept for the Sydney Opera House's iconic shells is most closely likened to what?
n: Utzon derived the geometry of the Opera House's iconic shells from segments of a sphere — famously likened to slices of an orange — solving the earlier construction difficulties of the free-form shells.
